System design interview clue: branches cost ~41 bytes, not “everything”.

• Snapshots, fingerprints & “sticker magic”: commits reference content by hash
• Zero full file copies: FILES COPIED = 0, COMMITS = 0—just pointers to blobs/tree objects
• Why branches are cheap: a new ref moves a pointer, not the whole history
• “One commit” model: commit object ties parent(s) + tree snapshot + metadata

Practical takeaway: Treat a commit like an immutable event in your architecture—content-addressing gives you dedupe + traceability.

If you want system design instincts, study Git internals: not as “version control,” but as a production-grade model for immutable content, references, and history.

Inside One Commit (what’s actually stored)
- Commit object: ties together parent commit(s), an associated tree snapshot, and metadata (author, timestamps, message).
- Tree object: represents directory structure for that snapshot.
- Blob object: represents file content. Content is addressed via cryptographic fingerprints (hashes).

Why branches are cheap (~41 bytes)
- A branch is essentially a movable reference (a ref) to a commit hash.
- Creating/changing a branch updates a pointer; it does not duplicate repository contents.
- That’s the architecture trade-off: you get fast “views” over immutable data with minimal overhead.

“Sticker magic” (dedupe by design)
- Because objects are identified by fingerprint, identical content maps to the same stored object.
- This makes history both space-efficient and audit-friendly—ideal for reasoning about causality (parent links) and correctness (hash integrity).

Production lesson to borrow for scalable backends & AI systems
- Prefer immutable artifacts + content-addressing when you need traceability, dedupe, caching, and safe concurrency.
- Model references (pointers/refs) as lightweight views over an immutable store.
